content: The remaining morbidity and mortality associated with HIV can be most effectively reduced by addressing specific stages of HIV care that contribute significantly to HIV-related deaths. This report identifies these critical stages based on observational studies linking mortality among HIV-positive adults to their prior HIV care and treatment experiences, as well as through mathematical modeling. Mathematical modeling was employed to project how the distribution of mortality across different stages of HIV care will evolve in the future. It also evaluated the potential impact of modifying antiretroviral therapy (ART) programs, specifically by changing eligibility criteria to allow immediate ART initiation without requiring a CD4 count. Empirical evidence from mortality surveillance is limited in generalized HIV epidemic settings due to the lack of comprehensive vital registration systems. To address this, two primary data sources were used to estimate the HIV care experiences of individuals dying from HIV in sub-Saharan Africa: general population cohort studies from the ALPHA network and linked vital registration and HIV care data from the Western Cape, South Africa. In the ALPHA network sites, the mortality rate among HIV-positive adults in 2011–2012 was approximately 25 per 1,000 person-years, representing a 3to 4-fold reduction from peak mortality levels. However, the majority of deaths in 2012 occurred among adults who had not initiated ART, except in uMkhanyakude, South Africa, where 40% of deaths occurred in individuals who had never started ART, 20% in those who recently initiated ART, and 40% in those on ART for more than six months. HIV-related mortality rates are highest among adults who have been on ART for less than six months or those who have disengaged from care or experienced treatment interruptions. However, these groups represent a small proportion of the HIV-positive population. The largest proportion of HIV-related deaths occurs among individuals who are ART-naïve, including those undiagnosed, diagnosed but not in care, or linked to care but not yet on ART. Mortality in these groups is significantly higher than in patients stable on ART for more than six months. In the Western Cape, South Africa, 3,161 HIV-positive adult deaths were recorded in 2012. Among these, 25% had no evidence of prior HIV care, 35% had a CD4 count test but never started ART, and 39% had previously been on ART. Late ART initiation, often due to delayed diagnosis and linkage to care, contributed to 34% of deaths among those who had been on ART for less than six months. Additionally, 32% of deaths occurred in individuals who had experienced gaps in ART treatment or disengaged from care. Mathematical models were developed for Rwanda, Kenya, Malawi, and South Africa to estimate HIV-related deaths across stages of care. These models were calibrated to national-level data on HIV prevalence, ART coverage, and care-seeking behaviors. They highlighted that between 30% and 50% of HIV-related deaths are projected to occur among individuals who never initiated ART, emphasizing the need for improvements in diagnosis, linkage to care, and ART initiation. Between 2004 and 2015, HIV-related deaths per 1,000 HIV-positive adults declined significantly in Rwanda (66%), Kenya (48%), Malawi (69%), and South Africa (44%) as ART programs were scaled up. However, a substantial proportion of deaths still occur among individuals who were never diagnosed or linked to care. In contrast, adults stable on ART for more than six months, who represent the largest share of the HIV-positive population, contribute a much smaller proportion of HIV-related deaths due to their lower mortality rates. Immediate ART initiation, regardless of CD4 count, has the potential to reduce HIV-related deaths further. Data from the Western Cape and mathematical models suggest that a significant proportion of deaths occur among individuals who were at one point linked to care but either never initiated ART or returned to care very late. Models estimate that 10% to 30% of HIV-related deaths in 2015 occurred in this group, underscoring the importance of timely ART initiation and retention in care.
